Beyond a 3-mile radius, the draft oxen hauling grain, turnip carts, and manure consume more calories in transit than their wagons deliver to market. overview: * The Stasis / The Lie: "The deep earth springs are inexhaustible and belong to everyone; no landlord can fence the rain that falls from heaven." * The Crucible / Conflict: A 90-day seasonal drought lowers the regional water table below the shaft floor; simultaneously, an upstream tanning pit dumps caustic arsenic broth into the hillside aquifer, sickening half the children in the village. * Dramatic Syllogism: * The Truth / Synthesis: Potable water is the invisible pivot of human sanity.
mechanical_architecture: Water is the absolute chronological ceiling of tabletop survival: a human body survives thirty days without food, but collapses into organ failure within three days without potable water. Pre-industrial settlements require 8–10 liters per adult daily for drinking and cooking, plus 30–50 liters daily per draft ox or plow horse. This mundane reality relies on three physical engineered elements: * The Dry-Stone Ashlar Shaft: Dug down 30–60 feet until reaching impermeable limestone bedrock or water-bearing gravel strata. Lined with dressed fieldstone bedded in slaked hydraulic lime mortar, preventing muddy surface seepage from contaminating the sweet deep groundwater. * The Counter-Weighted Timber Windlass: A heavy oak drum turned by iron crank handles, carrying hemp or rawhide rope coiled to drop two 5-gallon iron-banded buckets alternately.

mechanical_architecture: Pre-industrial economies do not run on shiny gold coins; ordinary peasants may go five years without seeing a single silver piece. Mundane survival is held together by two physical institutions: the charcoal-fired village forge and the weekly open-air barter square. These systems keep draft oxen working and allow households to exchange non-storable surpluses (eggs, fresh milk, churned butter) for durable staples (salt, homespun linen, iron nails): * The Charcoal Smithy: The technological beating heart of agriculture. A blacksmith does not forge legendary swords; they shoe sixteen plow horses every week, weld fractured iron plowshares, forge scythe blades, and draw nails from scrap iron billets. A settlement without a smith loses 40% of its harvesting capacity within a month due to broken cutting edges.

Atop the cairn sits an ancient, weather-beaten wooden icon carved from heart of oak, depicting the nameless ancestral protector who first cleared the valley. Passing travelers add a pebble to the cairn to pay respect and guarantee safe passage.
